title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 6
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The Invisible Network of Cold
passages.text:
A. Refrigeration is usually remembered as a domestic convenience, arriving in kitchens and changing how families shopped. The more consequential change happened before the kitchen and outside public view. Once perishable goods could be moved and stored cold, the geography of food production was released from the geography of consumption, and that release reorganised agriculture on a scale the household appliance did not approach.

B. The physical principle had been demonstrated well before commercial use. Compressing a gas and allowing it to expand absorbs heat, and mechanical systems exploiting this existed in laboratories decades before they appeared in ships or warehouses. What delayed adoption was not the science but reliability: early systems failed frequently, and a failure in a warehouse full of meat destroyed a cargo worth more than the equipment.

C. Long-distance shipment was the first commercially transformative application. Refrigerated vessels made it possible to sell meat and dairy produced on one continent to consumers on another, and the effect on producing regions was immediate — land that had supported extensive grazing for local markets acquired an export value it had never had. The effect on importing regions was equally sharp and less welcome to their own producers, who found themselves competing with distant land they could not outbid.

D. Distribution networks then grew around a requirement that is easy to state and hard to satisfy: the cold chain must be unbroken. A product held correctly for the whole journey and warmed for two hours at a transfer point may be indistinguishable in appearance from one handled properly, while carrying a materially different risk. This is why the industry's central problem has always been monitoring rather than cooling, and why the introduction of cheap continuous temperature logging changed practice more than any improvement in refrigeration efficiency.

E. Public health effects followed that are rarely credited to refrigeration. Reliable cold storage reduced foodborne illness substantially, and permitted vaccines and other temperature-sensitive medicines to reach populations that could not previously be supplied. In several countries the largest single obstacle to childhood immunisation has been the cold chain rather than the vaccine, and campaigns have failed for want of a working refrigerator at the last stage of a journey that was otherwise complete.

F. The environmental account is genuinely mixed and is often presented as though it were not. Refrigeration consumes a substantial share of global electricity, and the compounds used as refrigerants have included some with severe atmospheric effects, several now restricted. Against that, cold storage reduces food waste, and food that is grown and then discarded carries the whole environmental cost of its production for no benefit. Which side dominates depends on the electricity source and on how much waste is actually prevented, and confident statements in either direction usually rest on assumptions their authors have not examined.

passages.title: Predicting the Unpredictable
passages.text:
Seismologists distinguish between prediction and forecasting, and the distinction is not pedantry. A prediction specifies a place, a time window and a magnitude range with enough precision to justify action — evacuating a city, for instance. A forecast states a probability over a longer period. The first has not been achieved reliably for earthquakes and may not be achievable; the second is routine and underpins building codes across the world.

The reason for the asymmetry lies in the physics. Stress accumulates along faults over decades or centuries and is released when friction is overcome, but the point of release depends on conditions kilometres underground that cannot be observed directly and on the detailed geometry of rock that varies over short distances. Two faults with similar histories can behave entirely differently, and a small rupture and a great one begin identically — which is the central difficulty. If the beginning of a large earthquake is indistinguishable from the beginning of a small one, no warning system can tell them apart at the outset.

Precursors have been proposed repeatedly and have a poor record. Changes in groundwater chemistry, unusual animal behaviour, electromagnetic signals and patterns of small tremors have each been reported before significant events and have each failed to hold up when tested prospectively — that is, when used to make a prediction before rather than after the event. This distinction between retrospective and prospective testing is where most claimed precursors fail, since almost any signal can be found in the record once you know where to look.

What has succeeded is early warning, which is a different thing entirely and is frequently confused with prediction. Earthquakes generate fast, weak waves ahead of slower, damaging ones. A dense sensor network can detect the first and transmit an alert electronically faster than the second travels, giving seconds to tens of seconds of notice. That is enough to stop trains, close valves and halt surgery, and it is not prediction: the earthquake has already begun.

The social dimension has proved as difficult as the science. Warnings carry costs when wrong in both directions, and the asymmetry between them is not symmetrical in public perception. A false alarm that empties a city is expensive and erodes future compliance; a missed event is catastrophic. Officials issuing probabilistic statements have found them reported as certainties and, in one prominent case, faced legal consequences for reassurance that was scientifically defensible and disastrously interpreted.

The productive response has been to move effort away from prediction toward exposure. Building codes, retrofitting, land-use restriction and drills do not require knowing when an earthquake will happen, only that it will. This is undramatic and it is where essentially all measured reduction in earthquake mortality has come from — a fact that sits awkwardly with the continuing public appetite for a method of knowing in advance.

passages.title: The Making of Expertise
passages.text:
The proposition that expert performance is built by extended, structured practice rather than by innate gift became widely known through a simplification: that roughly ten thousand hours of practice produce mastery in any field. The underlying research says something more specific and considerably more useful, and the gap between the two has caused a decade of avoidable argument.

The original studies examined domains with stable rules, immediate feedback and established training traditions — chess, musical performance, competitive sport. Within those domains, accumulated hours of a particular kind of practice predicted attainment strongly. The kind mattered as much as the quantity. What was measured was not repetition but deliberate practice: working at the edge of current ability, on specific weaknesses, with feedback, usually under a teacher, and typically without enjoyment. Playing pieces one already performs well accumulates hours and produces little.

Subsequent work has narrowed the claim in two ways. First, the correlation, while real, leaves substantial variance unexplained — practice accounts for a meaningful share of the difference between performers and nothing close to all of it, and the share differs sharply by domain. It is largest in fields with stable rules and immediate feedback, and small in fields where neither holds. Second, the number itself was an average from one study of one instrument at one institution, and was never a threshold.

The domain dependence is the most practically important finding and the least widely repeated. Where feedback is delayed, ambiguous or absent, experience does not reliably produce expertise, and can produce confident error instead. Fields in which practitioners make judgements whose outcomes are unknown for years show weak or absent relationships between experience and accuracy, and in several the confidence of practitioners rises with experience while their accuracy does not. The problem is not the practitioners; it is that a domain without feedback cannot teach.

This yields a test that is more useful than counting hours. Ask whether the environment provides regular, unambiguous, timely information about whether a judgement was right. Where it does, deliberate practice works and experience is worth trusting. Where it does not, expertise in the ordinary sense may not be available at all, and the appropriate response is structural — checklists, statistical aids, decomposition of judgements into parts that can be verified — rather than more experience.

None of this restores the innate-talent account, which the evidence does not support in the form usually stated. What it replaces is the equally simple opposite: not everyone can reach elite performance through practice alone, practice quality matters more than practice quantity, and whether either matters at all depends on a property of the field rather than of the person.
